items.stem: How long is the previous-guide Paper 1 examination for both SL and HL?
items.answer: 1 hour (plus 5 minutes reading time)
items.markingKey: 1 hour (plus 5 minutes reading time). Paper 1 lasts one hour and carries 24 marks, with four questions on four sources.

items.stem: Distinguish between the message of a source and the content of a source.
items.answer: Content is what the source shows or says (figures, words, data); the message is the meaning or argument the creator intended, which must be inferred from the content in context.
items.markingKey: Content is what the source shows or says (figures, words, data); the message is the meaning or argument the creator intended, which must be inferred from the content in context. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Yusuf writes: "A cartoon has no value as evidence because it is exaggerated." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Exaggeration is part of a cartoon’s purpose; it is valuable evidence of contemporary opinion and of how events were perceived by the cartoonist and readers.
items.markingKey: Exaggeration is part of a cartoon’s purpose; it is valuable evidence of contemporary opinion and of how events were perceived by the cartoonist and readers. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Source A
Our countrymen have felt that we must abolish the evils of the present system and of the political parties. In Manchuria the army opened a way to the future of our nation. We have been driven to act because the government has been weak, and because the West has tried to block the natural development of Japan.
— Araki Sadao, Japanese army minister, radio broadcast to the nation, 1933 (paraphrased)

With reference to the origin, purpose and content of Source A, assess its values and limitations for historians investigating the move to global war, 1931–1940. [3]
items.answer: Value: It shows how a leading military figure and minister justified the Manchurian action to the Japanese public at the time. Limitations: As a broadcast by an army minister of the Kōdōha, it is intended to promote the army’s role and blame others; it is not an objective account of the decision-making in 1931.
items.markingKey: Value: It shows how a leading military figure and minister justified the Manchurian action to the Japanese public at the time. Limitations: As a broadcast by an army minister of the Kōdōha, it is intended to promote the army’s role and blame others; it is not an objective account of the decision-making in 1931. Award up to [3]: origin, purpose and content must each be referred to and linked to value or limitation for the stated enquiry. If only values or only limitations are discussed, award a maximum of [2]. Listing provenance without explaining its effect on value is not rewarded.

items.stem: Outline one way in which David Low’s cartoon “Stepping Stones to Glory” (Evening Standard, 8 July 1936) shows how symbols carry a cartoon’s message.
items.answer: Hitler walks up a staircase of figures labelled with British and French weaknesses such as “spinelessness” and “rearmament postponed”, while saluting. Each step is a symbol of Western weakness, so the message – that appeasers’ failings were enabling Hitler’s rise – comes from reading the labels in context.
items.markingKey: Context (Hitler walks up a staircase of figures labelled with British and French weaknesses such as “spinelessness” and “rearmament postponed”, while saluting.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Each step is a symbol of Western weakness, so the message – that appeasers’ failings were enabling Hitler’s rise – comes from reading the labels in context. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how symbols carry a cartoon’s message.

items.stem:
Source C
[Cartoon] A tiny Chinese figure lies on the ground while a Japanese soldier stands on him. Diplomats from Britain, France and the USA watch from a balcony labelled “Geneva”, discussing whether the soldier is “really standing on him or merely resting his foot”.
— Description of a cartoon published in the American magazine The Nation, 1932 (description adapted)

With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source C for an historian studying the move to global war, 1931–1940. [4]
items.answer: Value: It reveals a critical American view of the League’s legalistic response to Manchuria at the time of the Lytton enquiry. Limitations: A satirical, liberal magazine aimed at an American readership; it simplifies the diplomatic position and does not reflect the US government’s position.
items.markingKey: Value: It reveals a critical American view of the League’s legalistic response to Manchuria at the time of the Lytton enquiry. Limitations: A satirical, liberal magazine aimed at an American readership; it simplifies the diplomatic position and does not reflect the US government’s position. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "message (of a source)"?
options: Identifying ways in which two sources disagree or differ in their views, emphasis or evidence
A non-written source such as a cartoon, poster, photograph, map or table, whose message must be read from images, symbols and captions
Accurate, relevant historical information not contained in the sources, used to support, extend or challenge them
The main point or argument that the creator of a source intends to convey, inferred from its content, symbols and captions
items.answer: The main point or argument that the creator of a source intends to convey, inferred from its content, symbols and captions
items.markingKey: D. "message (of a source)" is the main point or argument that the creator of a source intends to convey, inferred from its content, symbols and captions.

items.stem: "The weakness of the League of Nations was the main reason why Japan was able to seize Manchuria in 1931–1932." How far do you agree with this statement? [15]
items.answer: League weakness removed an external restraint, but Japanese military initiative and Chinese weakness explain the seizure itself.
items.markingKey: Paper 3 essay. Indicative content: the League had no army and acted slowly (Lytton took a year); Britain and France were unwilling to impose sanctions; the USA and USSR were not members; the Kwantung Army’s initiative and Tokyo’s acceptance of the fait accompli; China’s weakness and Chiang’s priority of fighting the CCP; the Depression distracted all the powers. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: League weakness removed an external restraint, but Japanese military initiative and Chinese weakness explain the seizure itself. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "limitation (of a source)"?
options: The integration of evidence from sources with own knowledge into a single argument, rather than treating them separately
Identifying ways in which two sources disagree or differ in their views, emphasis or evidence
The ways in which the origin, purpose or content of a source restrict its usefulness for a particular enquiry
The ways in which a source is useful to an historian for a particular enquiry, arising from its origin, purpose and content
items.answer: The ways in which the origin, purpose or content of a source restrict its usefulness for a particular enquiry
items.markingKey: C. "limitation (of a source)" is the ways in which the origin, purpose or content of a source restrict its usefulness for a particular enquiry.

items.stem: A student claims that a primary source is always more valuable than a secondary source. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Value depends on the enquiry: a historian’s work may offer a wider view and access to archives, while a primary source gives contemporary perspective but may be partial.
items.markingKey: Value depends on the enquiry: a historian’s work may offer a wider view and access to archives, while a primary source gives contemporary perspective but may be partial. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why the date of a source matters when assessing its value.
items.answer: A source created at the time shows immediate perceptions without hindsight, but may lack information that emerged later; a later source may use more evidence but can be shaped by hindsight or the need to justify past actions.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A source created at the time shows immediate perceptions without hindsight, but may lack information that emerged later; a later source may use more evidence but can be shaped by hindsight or the need to justify past actions. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Source B
We have sustained a total and unmitigated defeat. All is over. Silent, mournful, abandoned, broken, Czechoslovakia recedes into the darkness. And do not suppose that this is the end. This is only the beginning of the reckoning.
— Winston Churchill, speech in the House of Commons during the debate on the Munich Agreement, 5 October 1938 (extract)

With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source B for an historian studying the move to global war, 1931–1940. [3]
items.answer: Value: It records the view of the most prominent Conservative critic of appeasement in Parliament at the time of the agreement. Limitations: Churchill was then a backbencher with a political interest in opposing Chamberlain; it is rhetorical and offers no evidence of Britain’s military position.
items.markingKey: Value: It records the view of the most prominent Conservative critic of appeasement in Parliament at the time of the agreement. Award up to [3]: origin, purpose and content must each be referred to and linked to value or limitation for the stated enquiry. items.stem: Outline one way in which the Hossbach Memorandum (1937) shows how origin affects the reliability of a document.
items.answer: Colonel Hossbach wrote up notes of Hitler’s meeting five days later, from memory; the surviving copy is a later transcript used at Nuremberg. Its value lies in recording Hitler’s private statements to his chiefs; its limitation is that it is an unofficial, delayed and copied record, which Taylor used to question its weight.
items.markingKey: Context (Colonel Hossbach wrote up notes of Hitler’s meeting five days later, from memory; the surviving copy is a later transcript used at Nuremberg.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Its value lies in recording Hitler’s private statements to his chiefs; its limitation is that it is an unofficial, delayed and copied record, which Taylor used to question its weight. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how origin affects the reliability of a document.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that the Munich Agreement was a defeat for Britain and France.
items.answer: In strategic terms Munich was a defeat, though the time gained for rearmament partly offset the losses.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Czechoslovakia lost its frontier defences and 35 divisions; Hitler gained the Sudetenland without war; the USSR was excluded and turned towards Germany. Arguments against: Britain gained a year to rearm (radar, fighters); British and Dominion opinion was united by 1939; Hitler felt cheated of his war in 1938. Supported judgement: In strategic terms Munich was a defeat, though the time gained for rearmament partly offset the losses.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why candidates should look for both explicit and implicit similarities when comparing sources.
items.answer: Sources from opposing perspectives may agree on facts (e.g. that Czechoslovakia was not consulted) while disagreeing on judgement; identifying implicit agreement shows deeper understanding. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)

items.stem:
Source C
The pact with Hitler was not simply a defensive move. By the secret protocol Stalin received eastern Poland, the Baltic states and Bessarabia. Stalin hoped the capitalist powers would exhaust one another in a long war while the USSR stood aside and expanded.
— Robert Service, British historian, Stalin: A Biography (2004) (paraphrased)

Identify three points made in Source C about appeasement and the outbreak of war in 1939. [3]
items.answer: The pact was not just defensive; the secret protocol gave Stalin large territories; Stalin hoped capitalist powers would weaken each other while the USSR expanded.
items.markingKey: The pact was not just defensive; the secret protocol gave Stalin large territories; Stalin hoped capitalist powers would weaken each other while the USSR expanded. Award 1 mark for each relevant point drawn from the source, up to [3]. Points must be taken from the source; own knowledge is not credited in Question 1.

items.stem: With reference to British and German press coverage of Munich (October 1938), explain how it illustrates how sources can agree on facts but differ in interpretation.
items.answer: The Daily Express proclaimed “Peace!” while the Völkischer Beobachter celebrated Hitler’s triumph and the return of the Sudeten Germans. Both reported that war had been avoided and the Sudetenland transferred, but the British paper stressed relief and peace while the German paper stressed national victory.
items.markingKey: Context (The Daily Express proclaimed “Peace!” while the Völkischer Beobachter celebrated Hitler’s triumph and the return of the Sudeten Germans.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Both reported that war had been avoided and the Sudetenland transferred, but the British paper stressed relief and peace while the German paper stressed national victory. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how sources can agree on facts but differ in interpretation.

items.stem: To what extent was the Soviet Union responsible for the outbreak of war in Europe in 1939? [15]
items.answer: The USSR enabled the war in 1939, but Hitler’s determination to attack Poland was the decisive factor.
items.markingKey: Paper 2 essay. Indicative content: Nazi–Soviet Pact and secret protocol; Western exclusion of the USSR at Munich; Hitler’s aims and Case White; British and French guarantees. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: The USSR enabled the war in 1939, but Hitler’s determination to attack Poland was the decisive factor. Source D
[Poster] A Japanese poster shows a samurai warrior with a sword standing over a snake labelled “ABCD” (America, Britain, China, Dutch) coiled around the Japanese islands. The caption reads: “Break the encirclement!”
— Description of a Japanese wartime propaganda poster, c. 1941–1942

With reference to the origin, purpose and content of Source D, assess its values and limitations for historians investigating the causes and outbreak of war in East Asia and Europe. [3]
items.answer: Value: It shows how the Japanese government justified the war to its people and the importance of the “encirclement” idea after the 1941 embargo. Limitations: As state propaganda it presents Japan as a victim and omits Japanese aggression in China and Indochina that provoked the embargo.

items.stem: Briefly describe a Question 4 on the success of appeasement and explain what it reveals about using contrasting sources and own knowledge to reach a judgement.

items.stem: With reference to the Hossbach Memorandum (1937), explain how it illustrates how origin affects the reliability of a document.
items.answer: Colonel Hossbach wrote up notes of Hitler’s meeting five days later, from memory; the surviving copy is a later transcript used at Nuremberg. Its value lies in recording Hitler’s private statements to his chiefs; its limitation is that it is an unofficial, delayed and copied record, which Taylor used to question its weight.

items.stem:
Source B
Japan cannot be blamed for seeking to secure its existence in a world that shut its doors on it. Although its methods were brutal, the war in the Pacific was the outcome of a long clash between Japanese ambitions in China and American determination to uphold the Open Door.
— Akira Iriye, Japanese-American historian, The Origins of the Second World War in Asia and the Pacific (1987) (paraphrased)

What, according to Source B, were the main features of the causes and outbreak of war in East Asia and Europe? [3]
items.answer: The war arose from a long-term clash between Japanese ambitions in China and US commitment to the Open Door; Japan’s search for security in a closed world is part of the explanation; Japan’s methods were brutal.

items.stem:
Source A
Our countrymen have felt that we must abolish the evils of the present system and of the political parties. In Manchuria the army opened a way to the future of our nation. We have been driven to act because the government has been weak, and because the West has tried to block the natural development of Japan.
— Araki Sadao, Japanese army minister, radio broadcast to the nation, 1933 (paraphrased)

Identify three points made in Source A about the move to global war, 1931–1940. [3]
items.answer: Japan needed to end the evils of party politics; the army’s action in Manchuria opened the nation’s future; weak government and Western obstruction forced Japan to act.

items.answer: Question 3 compares content: both similarities and differences in what the sources reveal must be identified and linked explicitly.

items.stem:
Source C
In the night of 18 September a detonation occurred on the railway. The Chinese soldiers had laid the charge. Our troops, few in number, were attacked and had no choice but to respond in self-defence, and within hours Mukden was secured.
— Report of the Kwantung Army headquarters to the General Staff in Tokyo, 19 September 1931 (paraphrased)

With reference to the origin, purpose and content of Source C, assess its values and limitations for historians investigating the move to global war, 1931–1940. [4]
items.answer: Value: It is the army’s own immediate account and shows how the incident was presented to Tokyo; it reveals the justification later used internationally. Limitations: Its purpose was to justify an unauthorised operation; the claim that Chinese soldiers laid the charge was false, as post-war testimony showed that Kwantung officers staged it.

items.stem: Compare and contrast the reasons for the outbreak of war in Europe in 1939 and in the Pacific in 1941. [15]
items.answer: Both wars stemmed from revisionist expansion, but in Europe appeasement enabled Hitler whereas in Asia US economic pressure forced Japan’s decision.
items.markingKey: Paper 2 essay. Indicative content: expansionist ideology in both Germany and Japan; appeasement in Europe vs economic pressure in Asia; role of the USSR and the USA; opportunism created by European war in 1940. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "corroboration"?
options: The reason a source was produced and the audience it was intended for, which affects what it includes and omits
A conclusion drawn from a source that goes beyond what it states directly, supported by details in the source
Accurate, relevant historical information not contained in the sources, used to support, extend or challenge them
The confirmation of a point in one source by other sources or by own knowledge
items.answer: The confirmation of a point in one source by other sources or by own knowledge
items.markingKey: D. "corroboration" is the confirmation of a point in one source by other sources or by own knowledge.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the message of a source and the content of a source.
items.answer: Content is what the source shows or says (figures, words, data); the message is the meaning or argument the creator intended, which must be inferred from the content in context.
items.markingKey: Content is what the source shows or says (figures, words, data); the message is the meaning or argument the creator intended, which must be inferred from the content in context. items.stem: Using Winston Churchill’s The Gathering Storm (1948) as an example, explain how purpose affects the value of a memoir.
items.answer: Churchill’s memoir presented the 1930s as a story of avoidable disaster caused by appeasers, while he had warned of the danger. It is valuable for the views of a leading critic of appeasement, but written after the war partly to vindicate his own record, so it underplays the constraints Chamberlain faced.

items.stem: With reference to David Low’s cartoon “Stepping Stones to Glory” (Evening Standard, 8 July 1936), explain how it illustrates how symbols carry a cartoon’s message.
items.answer: Hitler walks up a staircase of figures labelled with British and French weaknesses such as “spinelessness” and “rearmament postponed”, while saluting. Each step is a symbol of Western weakness, so the message – that appeasers’ failings were enabling Hitler’s rise – comes from reading the labels in context.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that the Munich Agreement was a defeat for Britain and France.
items.answer: In strategic terms Munich was a defeat, though the time gained for rearmament partly offset the losses.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Czechoslovakia lost its frontier defences and 35 divisions; Hitler gained the Sudetenland without war; the USSR was excluded and turned towards Germany. Arguments against: Britain gained a year to rearm (radar, fighters); British and Dominion opinion was united by 1939; Hitler felt cheated of his war in 1938. Supported judgement: In strategic terms Munich was a defeat, though the time gained for rearmament partly offset the losses.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that the war in the Pacific in 1941 was caused by US economic pressure on Japan?
items.answer: US pressure precipitated the decision, but Japan’s refusal to abandon expansion was the underlying cause.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: oil embargo and asset freeze of July–August 1941; Hull Note seen as an ultimatum; encirclement propaganda in Japan. Arguments against: Japanese aggression in China since 1937 and in Indochina caused the embargo; Tripartite Pact aligned Japan with Germany; Japanese leaders chose war over withdrawal. Supported judgement: US pressure precipitated the decision, but Japan’s refusal to abandon expansion was the underlying cause.
